Succulent Poaching

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Succulent Poaching syndicates taking over from Rhino poaching in South Africa

Unique Selling Point:
In the last two years there has been a dramatic increase in succulent poaching in South Africa despite their being fewer foreign visitors in the country, but lockdown around the world has in fact driven the demand for exotic succulents for people to cultivate on their windowsills. The Asian market has latched onto conopyhtum succulents as their latest fad which grow in the vast open stretches of the Karoo, the Richtersveld and even as far south as the Robertson in the Western Cape. These wild arid places make easy pickings for poachers. They are harvesting 1000s of plants at a time, and these plants grown is such specific conditions adapted to their unique environment and are extremely localise, their range can be the size of a rugby field. And like all things the more rare the more valuable, these tiny succulents are pound for pound as valuable as drugs and rhino horn

Summary:
Sussana Holtz lives on a farm outside Worcester close to the busy N1. When they moved there, they thought they would have to restore the wild animals that had been hunted out by locals hunting dogs, little did they realise they would have to protect the plants as well. To date they have got 12 people arrested and charged for collecting over 3000 conophytum on their little koppie, the street value is estimated to be R1,5 million, and there are signs that the poaching continues.
The poaches have been driven as far south as the Robertson/ Worcester area because the policing of the succulent poachers has become more effective up north, and locally farmers are unaware of the scourge, so when they find people on their farms saying they just Rastas collecting muti they get off with a warning not to trespass
But what’s great about this story is that because Sussanah was so proactive they have got the local head of the Stock and endangered species protection unit, to return the stolen plants that are not part of any the ongoing case. Specialist succulent botanist Ernst Van Jarsveld who established the Kirstenbosch succulent herbarium and has now done the same at Babylonstoren came to the farm to see if these succulents could be replanted on the mountain where the farmer could keep an eye on them. To their delight they did, and I have filmed them replanting over 500 plants that are over 200 years old, back in their habitat. But this is extremely rare because mostly they are intercepting plants at the airport. After they have to identified them and usually have no idea where they came from, those are likely to die or be cultivated in a nursery, but lost to the wild.


Further information:
Local poaching syndicates are buying them up and couriering them out the country. Fortunately, they being detected, 22 000 plants were intercepted at the airport in the last month alone. Returning these stolen plants to their original locations is near impossible because we often have no idea where they come from, and they so specifically adapted to grown in particular conditions you can’t just plant them anywhere. Kirstenbosch and the Karoo succulent garden in Worcester is overflowing with confiscated succulents.
The dramatic increase in poaching is driving botanists to behave like under cover-agents unwilling to go on camera, jealously guarding the locations of these rare plants and ensuring they don’t share any GPS co-ordinates of their findings in scientific journals and popular scientific sites like INaturalists because the poachers scourge these sites and send the information to the collectors on the ground. The collectors are local Rastas or simply farm workers or people who live in these remote locations with very little chance of any other income. But the disturbing factor is when plant enthusiast, people who know how rare they are act as tour guides to foreign collectors and take them into these remote locations.
I have the pictures of the people arrested on the farm, and their haul. I have Nico Du Toit unpacking one of the boxes that was intercepted at the airport. I also have video of the collectors showing what they have stolen bidding to buyers. I hope to get into the airport or get Nico to film that. On 19th July a local succulent expert David Cumming will be sentenced in the Cape Town court for acting as a tour guide for American nursery succulent collector Kalman Kaminar. Kaminar was arrested with 354 rare plants and sentenced to two years in jail, suspended for 5 years and banned from the country. He paid a R500 000 fine.

Nico: Here we have a box was seized at the airport it was on its way to Hong Kong. They scanned they scan all the boxes and detected that there are some plants inside the box……..... Its filled with toy boxes Last month we had cases like once or twice a week, there was nearly 22000 clusters, 11 different species of conophytums that is over a month period

Script: Syndicates scoure academic papers where GPS coordinates are regularly sighted, and popular scientific websites have had to removed GPS locations after poaches admitted to using them

Corne: what I find sad is often it's people involved who have got intimate knowledge of these plants and one would expect someone who studied these plants, a lifelong, uh, would cherish and protect these plants, but often they exploit it purely for commercial and financial gain.

Script: A case in point is David Cumming, a local enthusiast who has succulents named after him. He acted as a tour guide for foreign plant collectors. He was arrested and found guilty with American plant collector Kalman Kaminarn, in possession of 337 protected plants. Kaminarn was fined R500 000 and given a 5 year suspended sentence and deported. Cumming is awaiting sentence

Link: One would think you could just replant them but they grow in such specific locations, adapted to survive in extreme conditions, so you can’t just randomly pop plants back into similar habitats

Ernst: There is many of these little conophytums that we have no idea, they have been confiscated. And to just guess and just to replant them anywhere is not going to help. And if they don't get planted soon and in the right place where they will flourish, they will die. And at the moment, there is too many to to handle.

Script: But the good news is that conophytum produce hundreds of seeds. The forensic botanist harvested seed from confiscated plants that come from one specific area, and hopes to reseed them there. He also plans to share seed internationally with growers, to reduce their value and the demand of wild plants. But currently, he just doesn’t have the people power, so in the meantime, he is reviving the last 12 000 conophytum concavum on earth

Adam they often arrive like this in the forensic bags and they look virtually dead. we nurture them and then eventually they revive themselves and they come back to life.

Script: Given the dire lack of resources its up to the vigilance and commitment of farmers like Holtz and her husband to protect our heritage

Susannah It's just a matter of putting a line in the ground about what is and is not acceptable in terms of what is for sale in the country you know and what is sacred?

Script: She was delighted when Du Toit returned the plants which were not part of an ongoing case, and brought Van Jaarsveldt with him to search for a safer site. Together they all climbed the mountain and were overjoyed to find them in a spot they could keep their eye on. It was one of the first times poached plants could be replanted from where they were stolen, lifting everyone's hearts.

Corne: it's a bit of a glimmer of hope in what often seems hopeless,

And at the moment, there is too many to to handle. Script: But the good news is that conophytum produce hundreds of seeds. The forensic botanist harvested seed from confiscated plants that come from one specific area, and hopes to reseed them there. He also plans to share seed internationally with growers, to reduce their value and the demand of wild plants. But currently, he just doesn’t have the people power, so in the meantime, he is reviving the last 12 000 conophytum concavum on earth Adam they often arrive like this in the forensic bags and they look virtually dead. we nurture them and then eventually they revive themselves and they come back to life. Script: Given the dire lack of resources its up to the vigilance and commitment of farmers like Holtz and her husband to protect our heritage Susannah It's just a matter of putting a line in the ground about what is and is not acceptable in terms of what is for sale in the country you know and what is sacred? Script: She was delighted when Du Toit returned the plants which were not part of an ongoing case, and brought Van Jaarsveldt with him to search for a safer site. Together they all climbed the mountain and were overjoyed to find them in a spot they could keep their eye on. It was one of the first times poached plants could be replanted from where they were stolen, lifting everyone's hearts. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Succulent Poaching syndicates taking over from Rhino poaching in South Africa
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the last two years there has been a dramatic increase in succulent poaching in South Africa despite their being fewer foreign visitors in the country, but lockdown around the world has in fact driven the demand for exotic succulents for people to cultivate on their windowsills. The Asian market has latched onto conopyhtum succulents as their latest fad which grow in the vast open stretches of the Karoo, the Richtersveld and even as far south as the Robertson in the Western Cape. These wild arid places make easy pickings for poachers. They are harvesting 1000s of plants at a time, and these plants grown is such specific conditions adapted to their unique environment and are extremely localise, their range can be the size of a rugby field. And like all things the more rare the more valuable, these tiny succulents are pound for pound as valuable as drugs and rhino horn
metadata.Summary: Sussana Holtz lives on a farm outside Worcester close to the busy N1. When they moved there, they thought they would have to restore the wild animals that had been hunted out by locals hunting dogs, little did they realise they would have to protect the plants as well. To date they have got 12 people arrested and charged for collecting over 3000 conophytum on their little koppie, the street value is estimated to be R1,5 million, and there are signs that the poaching continues. The poaches have been driven as far south as the Robertson/ Worcester area because the policing of the succulent poachers has become more effective up north, and locally farmers are unaware of the scourge, so when they find people on their farms saying they just Rastas collecting muti they get off with a warning not to trespass But what’s great about this story is that because Sussanah was so proactive they have got the local head of the Stock and endangered species protection unit, to return the stolen plants that are not part of any the ongoing case. Specialist succulent botanist Ernst Van Jarsveld who established the Kirstenbosch succulent herbarium and has now done the same at Babylonstoren came to the farm to see if these succulents could be replanted on the mountain where the farmer could keep an eye on them. To their delight they did, and I have filmed them replanting over 500 plants that are over 200 years old, back in their habitat. But this is extremely rare because mostly they are intercepting plants at the airport. After they have to identified them and usually have no idea where they came from, those are likely to die or be cultivated in a nursery, but lost to the wild.
metadata.Further information: Local poaching syndicates are buying them up and couriering them out the country. Fortunately, they being detected, 22 000 plants were intercepted at the airport in the last month alone. Returning these stolen plants to their original locations is near impossible because we often have no idea where they come from, and they so specifically adapted to grown in particular conditions you can’t just plant them anywhere. Kirstenbosch and the Karoo succulent garden in Worcester is overflowing with confiscated succulents. The dramatic increase in poaching is driving botanists to behave like under cover-agents unwilling to go on camera, jealously guarding the locations of these rare plants and ensuring they don’t share any GPS co-ordinates of their findings in scientific journals and popular scientific sites like INaturalists because the poachers scourge these sites and send the information to the collectors on the ground. The collectors are local Rastas or simply farm workers or people who live in these remote locations with very little chance of any other income. But the disturbing factor is when plant enthusiast, people who know how rare they are act as tour guides to foreign collectors and take them into these remote locations. I have the pictures of the people arrested on the farm, and their haul. I have Nico Du Toit unpacking one of the boxes that was intercepted at the airport. I also have video of the collectors showing what they have stolen bidding to buyers. I hope to get into the airport or get Nico to film that. On 19th July a local succulent expert David Cumming will be sentenced in the Cape Town court for acting as a tour guide for American nursery succulent collector Kalman Kaminar. Kaminar was arrested with 354 rare plants and sentenced to two years in jail, suspended for 5 years and banned from the country. He paid a R500 000 fine.
